title: Define the decision before the search
facts: A fictional clinic currently offers usual follow-up. It is considering a home-monitoring programme that also requires extra clinic visits. A frail adult asks whether it is worth joining to avoid hospital admissions over the next year.
q: Which question best matches this person’s comparative decision?
options: In adults receiving monitoring, how accurately do device readings predict subsequent admission over one year?
In adults with similar frailty, how does monitoring compare with another device for one-year biomarker control?
In adults with similar frailty, how does the programme compare with usual follow-up for one-year admissions and visit burden?
In adults receiving usual follow-up, which baseline characteristics predict one-year admission most accurately?
In adults across all age groups, how does monitoring change attendance at scheduled appointments over one year?
notes: This is a prediction question about the device, not the comparative offer of the whole programme.
It changes both comparator and outcome, leaving the patient's admission and burden question unresolved.
This preserves the relevant population, programme contrast, outcome, burden and one-year horizon.
Prognosis can inform baseline risk but does not compare programme benefits and burdens.
Attendance and a broad age population do not fully answer this frail person's admission decision.

title: Translate the effect to a different baseline risk
facts: A fictional randomised trial reports admissions at one year in 20/100 usual-care participants and 10/100 programme participants. The clinician estimates this person's usual-care admission risk at 4%. For this arithmetic exercise only, assume the trial's relative effect transfers unchanged.
q: Under that assumption, what absolute benefit and NNT follow for this person’s baseline risk?
options: ARR 10 percentage points; NNT 10 over one year
ARR 4 percentage points; NNT 25 over one year
ARR 50 percentage points; NNT 2 over one year
ARR 1 percentage point; NNT 100 over one year
ARR 2 percentage points; NNT 50 over one year
notes: This imports the trial's absolute reduction despite a different baseline risk.
This uses the entire baseline risk as the reduction, as if the treated risk were zero.
This converts the 50% relative reduction directly into percentage points.
This would follow from a 25% relative reduction at baseline risk 4%, not the stated 50% reduction.
Trial RR is 0.10/0.20 = 0.5. Applied to 4%, treated risk is 2%; ARR is 2 points and NNT is 1/0.02 = 50.

title: Put the absolute benefit beside a preference
facts: The patient understands the estimates and says that, given the travel burden, joining would be worthwhile only for at least a three-percentage-point reduction in one-year admission risk. Continue using the preceding transport assumption; this is a fictional values exercise, not a clinical recommendation.
q: Which interpretation correctly relates the calculated point benefit to this stated threshold?
options: The 50% relative reduction exceeds a three-point absolute threshold.
The implied two-point absolute reduction is below the stated minimum.
The trial's ten-point absolute reduction is the relevant value for this patient.
The NNT of 50 means the patient gains 50 percentage points of protection.
The treated risk of 2% is itself the size of the relative reduction.
notes: The quantities are on different scales; relative percentage reduction cannot be compared directly with an absolute-point threshold.
The assumed individual-context ARR is 4% − 2% = 2 percentage points. A stated three-point minimum is not met by that point estimate; uncertainty and preferences still belong in discussion.
That value belongs to the trial's 20% baseline risk and was not the translated absolute effect.
NNT is a reciprocal group effect measure, not a percentage-point benefit for an individual.
Two percent is the treated event risk under the assumption, while relative reduction is 50%.
